A gate of two bent hazel wands pegged into the stream bed, a fat rose-hip hung at the crown on a grass line, drooping low enough that every mast must duck, the left peg already tilting in the silt.

The turn marker: a rowanberry the colour of fire tethered to a sunken flint by a braid of reed-grass, bobbing hard in the current, a dragonfly riding it steadily in the opposite direction the race runs.

A start arch of two bulrush stems leaning from opposite banks, their tips lashed at the peak with sedge cord, a single dewdrop hung at the crossing on a milkweed-floss strand, swelling fat and ready to be struck.

The run's end: a garland of linked clover heads strung between two listing reeds above the surface, sagging to touch the water at its middle, four clover heads already chewed to bare stalks by something working from the left.

A count-twig of peeled birch laid across a mossy stone, nine river pebbles arranged along it, three knocked to the far end already, one sitting an inch below in the shallows where it rolled and nobody has fetched it back.

A gate of arched bramble shoot pegged into the gravel, a hawthorn berry hung dead centre on a grass thread, the berry so low a tall acorn-cap mast cannot pass without tilting, and a pale mayfly perched on the berry itself.

A second gate deeper on the course, its two reed-wand posts lashed with pine-resin to anchor stones, the crosspiece a length of plaited grass gone crooked mid-span where the resin dripped too thin and the cord slipped.

A mid-course gate of bent willow-withe, both peg ends tied to submerged pebbles, a loop of grass at the crown with one small elderberry dangling, spinning slowly in the eddy, the elderberry staining the current a faint wine-purple beneath.

A turn-post of a single cattail stem pushed into soft mud, a ring of woven rush near its base to hold it from tilting, the ring having tilted anyway, and a pond-snail climbing the stem in the wrong direction.

A signal drum of a large acorn cap lashed mouth-upward to a hazel stake at the bank, a beater of moss-wrapped grass beside it, and a scatter of last year's petals blown into the drumhead and softening the skin.

The second turn: a rose-hip on a braided sedge line pegged to a flat stone, a second smaller hip tied below the first for ballast, both hips spinning together in the current like a tiny double lantern.

A gate whose arch is a fresh bracken stem, still curling green at its tip, bent in a wide loop and both ends pressed into the bed with split-twig pegs, a single cranberry bead hung at its crown by a grass fibre.

The finish: a strand of dandelion-down stretched between two upright reed stems, both stems leaning inward from the pressure of the strand, so the whole gate tilts like a doorway in a storm and the down shimmers in the current's breath.

A checkpoint of two crossed twig wands lashed with rush cord forming an X above the water, a dried violet hanging at their crossing, its purple still vivid, stem looped through the lashing and one petal already detached, drifting downstream.

A half-gate for the shallows: one hazel wand bent from the bank and pegged into the opposite side with its tip only, a loop of grass trailing from the bend holding a rowanberry, the whole arm bowing lower as the flow pushes.

A pebble-count station: a flat stone the size of three boats, a peeled reed laid across its face, eleven small pale river pebbles along its length, and a slender fae in woven-grass clothes kneeling to move the fifth pebble with both hands.

A warning-post before the sharp bend: a tall bulrush pushed into the mud bank at a lean, a braid of bent grass wound around its midsection and tied off with a knot the size of an acorn, a dew-bead caught in the knot.

A gate of two green ash-keys bent into an arch, their own natural curl doing half the shaping, a red campion petal draped over the crown as a hanging marker, the petal folded once and held by a single thread of reed-fibre.

A finish-alternative garland of apple-blossom heads linked by their own stems, strung between two leaning reeds barely a thumb above the water, a bumblebee's weight already bending the third bloom down to kiss the surface intermittently.

A gust-chime of five empty hazelnut shells threaded on a single length of rush cord and hung from a low alder branch over the water, rattling together in the slightest draught to call the start fae to readiness on the bank.

The halfway point of the course shown by one fat rose-hip wedged between two forked twigs pushed into the bed and bound with pine resin, the hip glossy red and half under water, one twig already bowing downstream in the current.

A second signal post with an acorn-cap drum lashed above water-height to a willow stake, its beater a knob of soft moss on a hazel splint, the whole stake canted five degrees off true where the bank gave after last rain.

A gate repaired in the night: two reed posts with a crosspiece of bent grass cord, a visible binding of doubled rush at the mend, and a fresh rowanberry re-hung there to replace one that vanished, its grass tether still showing a pale raw knot.

The inner turn of the loop: a walnut shell weighted with a chip of flint, tethered on a plaited sedge line to a submerged root, rocking in the eddy, a water-boatman sitting perfectly still on its rim as though it owns the course.

A counting stone beside the bank: a broad flat grey pebble standing upright in the mud, eleven smaller white pebbles laid in a row along its top edge, one teetering at the far end, held from falling by a sprig of dried thyme.

A gate of two hazel-twig arches pegged into the gravel bed, a single sloe-berry hung at the centre on grass cord, so low that every passing mast bows under it like a courtier, one peg already tilting.

The start: two bulrush stems bent inward from opposite banks and lashed at their crossing, a fat dewdrop suspended there on a hair-thin root, swinging, a single mayfly perched on the knot and refusing to move.

The run's end: a garland of linked clover heads strung between two leaning reeds, sagging badly at the middle, four clover heads already eaten to bare stalks, the strand thin enough that a drifting oak leaf spans the whole channel beneath it.

A tethered rose-hip the colour of cooling embers, moored to a half-buried river pebble on a plaited grass line, marking the first turn, spinning slowly in the current with a necklace of white foam caught around its stem.

A count-twig of peeled birch laid across a flat moss-stone, eight acorn cups ranged along it for the boats passing through, three cups knocked sideways already, one sitting in the shallows below where the current took it.

A second gate, its left arch mended mid-span with a bright knot of grass cord after the twig split, a rowanberry hung at the join instead of the centre because that is where the cord was long enough to reach.

A strand of dandelion-down strung between two upright reed-stems, marking the final run, floating and sinking with each breath of moving air, a water-strider standing directly beneath it as though appointed to watch.

A starting drum of two acorn caps fitted rim-to-rim and lashed to a hazel stake, its moss-padded beater leaning against the stake, a slender palm-sized fae in leaf-cloth kneeling beside it with one fist raised and ready.

A turning post of a single pine cone skewered onto a sharpened reed and pushed into the stream bed, leaning ten degrees downstream, a grass line tethering it to a root so it does not finish the race ahead of anyone.

A lane divider of threaded rowanberries knotted at thumb-width intervals along a grass cord stretched bank to bank, three berries missing from the middle run where something ate through the night and left only the knots.

A mid-course arch of a bent alder twig pegged at both banks, hung with a chain of apple-blossom threading bank to bank, the whole arch low enough that a tall fern frond overhangs it like a second roof pressing down.

A pebble-count station: a smooth river stone with a groove worn along its top, nine hazelnut-shell halves set in the groove for the boats passing, a palm-sized fae in petal-silk lying flat on the stone to peer through the gate below.

A turn marker of a fat green acorn still in its cap, tethered by a plait of grass to a submerged stone the size of a sleeping vole, bobbing and ducking, a small beetle riding its crown with its legs braced.

A false gate, built as a joke-trap at the wide bend: two cattail stems crossed overhead trailing hung leaf-triangles, the gap between them barely wider than a walnut shell, mended once already with a twist of root.

A bridge-gate of a single curved birch-bark strip pegged bank to bank, its belly hanging a finger above the waterline, a dragonfly gripping its upper edge and holding so still it looks like the decoration was intentional.

An elapsed-count rack of a peeled willow sliver propped between two stones, with seven small white quartz chips laid along it and a slender fae in woven-grass cloth sitting cross-legged beside it, moving one chip left with every boat that passes.

A boundary reed-post: one tall bulrush pushed deep into the mud at the channel's edge, a chain of linked clover heads wound twice around its stem and trailing into the current, one clover head opening and closing in the flow like a slow fist.
A hanging turn-signal of a single dried rose-hip split open to show its seeds inside, suspended on a doubled grass cord from a low alder branch, spinning freely over the water, one seed already gone.

A course marker of an upturned snail shell pegged to the stream bed on a sharpened twig, its spiral pointing skyward, a plait of grass tethering it to the bank so it only travels in small urgent circles.

A waypost of a seed-pod split and opened flat on a reed stake, its inner white lining catching light, planted at the mid-channel shallows where a river pebble the height of three boats rises from the gravel like a grey cliff.

A second count-stone downstream, a slab of pale shale with ten acorn caps in a row along its top, a fae in moss-velvet kneeling at one end with a twig as a pointer, one cap already sailing away on its own small current.

A start-line marker of two hazel rods driven into opposite banks at the same angle, a threaded chain of violet petals strung taut between them, one rod already bowing downstream, the petals sagging into a low smile.

A mid-course turn buoy of a walnut half-shell weighted with a chip of quartz and tethered by grass cord to a buried twig, rolling in the current, a water-boatman sheltering in its hollow from the wash of passing hulls.

A gate of two pine-resin-stiffened grass stems arching from the stream bed, a single hawthorn berry hung at the apex on a loop of root, the left stem leaning after the mud gave, the berry now off-centre and lower on that side.

An end-gate of bent reed forming a low arch, hung with a plait of meadowgrass trailing into the water, a fat frog planted on the bank directly beside it, sitting with such settled authority the plait swings across its nose with every boat that passes.

A distance post of a broad sycamore seed pinned upright in the shallows on a sharpened twig, its paired wing spreading over the channel like a low sail, a thread of moss-cord keeping it from spinning into the current.

A course divider of a single long grass stem laid flat across the water from bank to bank, one end pegged under a stone, the other tied to a bent rush, the whole length dipping and rising as the current breathes under it.

A winner's stone: a polished river pebble placed on a flat shale shelf at the water's edge, a woven ring of clover laid around it, a single fae in birch-bark sandals sitting on the shelf behind it with both hands folded, waiting.

A signal chime of three dewdrops threaded on a hair-thin root tied between two reed-stems, each drop a different size, the smallest still forming, a fae in leaf-cloth standing beside them with a twig striker, not yet touching.

A final gate of two cattail wands crossed overhead and pegged into the gravel, a garland of linked clover looped at the crossing and already half unwound downstream, one end trailing the current like a long slow thought going somewhere else.
A gate of two hazel switches bent into an arch over the current, a single sloe berry hung at the crown on a grass thread, so low that every mast must lean sideways to duck under it.
Two bulrush stems crossed and lashed at the tips with grass cord above the water, a fat dewdrop strung at the crossing on a root-hair, ready to be struck, one stem already bowing under the weight.
The turn marker: a rowanberry the colour of a struck match tethered on braided grass to a sunken stone, bobbing hard in the flow, a damselfly gripping it and riding each dip without letting go.

A garland of linked clover heads strung between two leaning reeds above the channel, sagging low enough to graze the tallest mast-tip, four clover heads eaten down to bare stalk from the left side inward.
A count-twig of peeled ash laid across a flat river stone, ten small pebbles ranged along it in a row, two already moved to the far end, one tipped into the shallows where a passing hull knocked it.

An acorn-cap drum lashed to a hazel stake at the bank's edge, a moss-padded beater leaning against it, a slender palm-sized fae in leaf-cloth crouching beside it with one hand raised and her pointed ears forward.

A midcourse gate of two birch-bark strips bent into a narrow arch, pegged with forked twigs into the gravel bed, a rose-hip hung at the arch's centre trailing a bright thread of foam where the current catches it.

A tethered walnut-shell buoy filled with white quartzite sand so it rides low and heavy, anchored on a moss-cord to a buried acorn, bobbing in slow circles, a water-snail making steady progress around its equator.

The final gate: two elder twigs woven into an oval frame and staked upright in the shallows, a chain of apple-blossom looped across its opening, petals already loosening and spinning away one at a time downstream.

A turning post of a single cattail stem driven into the bed with a split-reed streamer spiralling from its tip, the stem listing twelve degrees because the mud below was softer than the setter guessed.

A course marker of stacked hazelnuts threaded on a root-hair around a reed stake, each nut at a different height, the top one cracked open and a violet moth-wing pressed inside facing outward like a painted eye.

A grass-cord lane divider strung between two pegged sticks barely a thumb above the water, threaded with alternate rowanberries and dry seedpods, sagging in the middle so the cord drags the surface and catches every passing hull-tip.

The finish strand: a single thread of dandelion-down stretched between two upright reeds tied at chest height, gleaming and trembling in the air, one end already pulling free where the reed it is knotted to has begun to topple.
A bent-twig arch mended at its crown with a tight wrapping of grass cord over a fresh crack, a hawthorn berry hanging from the repair on a root-hair as if the mending itself chose its own ornament.

A turn stone: one river pebble the height of three boats standing on its end in the shallows, balanced against a wedge of bark, a fat frog sitting pressed flat against its upstream face holding perfectly still.

A midstream gate of two curved fern-frond stems arching toward each other, their tips tied with moss-cord, a dried violet petal dangling between them on a grass thread, the petal twirling steadily in the current's breath.

A plait of three grass strands stretched between pegged sticks across the narrow channel, threaded with five linked clover heads at equal intervals, the centre clover head sitting in the water because the cord gave half a thumb.

A course peg of a forked willow twig driven upright into the bank, a chain of threaded blackthorn berries looped between its two tines, the whole thing leaning upstream so the berry chain swings permanently to one side.

A starting arch of two green reeds bent inward from opposite banks and lashed together at the top, a dew-filled acorn cap hanging at the junction on a root-hair thread, swinging freely and catching what light reaches the water.

A count-stone of grey slate laid flat on a mossy bank step, a peeled twig across it, eight pebbles waiting in a line, a slender fae in woven-grass tunic kneeling over it with a ninth pebble pinched ready.

Two seed-pods of honesty, flat as coins, threaded onto a grass strand and strung across the channel as a mid-course marker, each pod a pale paper circle trembling in the airflow from the water, one split along its seam.

A turning post of a stripped elderberry stem lashed to a stone anchor with moss-cord, a sprig of dried heather bound to its top, the whole post titled at an angle so the heather drags the surface on the downstream side.

A gate pegged into the gravel with one twig arm longer than the other, giving the arch a lopsided grin, a single scarlet rose-hip hung not at the crown but at the shorter side, bumping every hull that threads too close.

A finish garland of threaded hawthorn berries and oak-gall beads strung between two tall reeds, one reed leaning so far the garland dips to a deep V, the low point skimming the water with each gust from the bank.

A signal drum of a half-walnut shell stretched over with a dried violet-petal membrane, lashed to a rush stake, a beater of a twig tipped with moss, a palm-sized fae in petal-silk tunic standing behind it with both eyes forward.

A tethered hazelnut shell weighted with river clay and anchored on a root-hair, spinning slowly in the current, the hinge-scar on its side painted with a single curved crescent of elderberry juice the colour of a bruise.

A lane divider of a grass-cord strung taut between two forked-twig stakes, hung with a row of birch-bark triangles folded and threaded at intervals, three triangles facing upstream and one turned the wrong way round by the setter's mistake.

The prize stone: a river pebble ground smooth and left on a flat outcrop just above the water, a woven clover wreath laid around it, one bee still buried head-first in a clover head and unaware the race has almost reached it.

A midcourse marker of a folded sycamore-key wing pinned upright to a rush stake with a thorn, the wing's natural spiral making it spin in the current's breath, a reed warbler gripping the stake below it and watching downstream.

A gate of two curved rush stems forming an oval doorway above the channel, a chain of threaded apple-blossom across its mouth at mast height, the lowest bloom already dropping petals that spin away in the wake of the leading hull.

A gate of two hazel twigs bent arch-wise and pegged into the gravel, a single sloe-berry hung at its crown on a grass thread, so low that every mast must bow — one peg already tilting, the arch listing starboard.

The start: two bulrush stems leaned in from opposite banks and knotted at the crossing with rush cord, a fat dewdrop suspended there on a hair-thin root, trembling, ready for the striker's tap, one stem shorter than the other.

A turn-marker: a rose-hip the deep red of old embers, tethered by grass cord to a sunken stone, bobbing in the channel's pull, a thread of white foam curling behind it, one end of the cord already half unravelled.

The run's end: a garland of clover heads threaded on a split grass stem and strung between two leaning reeds a finger above the water, four of the heads already nibbled to bare stalks by a passing water-vole.

A count-twig: a peeled birch wand laid across a mossy stone beside the bank, nine river pebbles ranked along it, five moved to the far end, one teetering at the edge where the stone slopes into the stream.

A second gate mid-channel built from one forked willow switch driven into the silt, the fork holding a threaded chain of apple-blossom tight across the gap, the whole frame tilted fifteen degrees downstream by the current's nudge.

A warning arch of bent grass stems plaited into a low hoop over the narrowing, a dried seed-pod rattle lashed at its crown so every mast that catches it makes the whole thing shiver and the pod clatter.

A tethered snail shell the size of a cartwheel to the fae fleet, anchored on a grass line to a half-buried pebble, spinning slow in the eddy and trailing a coil of milkweed floss like a wandering wake.

A re-start bell: a hollow hazelnut shell suspended mouth-down from a reed tripod, a polished river pebble on a root thread hanging inside it, the whole tripod leaning until the pebble just grazes the shell and rings at every ripple.

The half-way post: a single cattail stem driven upright into the bank-mud, a chain of threaded rowanberries wound twice around it and dangling in a loop over the water, two berries already knocked free and bobbing downstream.

A low bridge-gate of one flat alder leaf pinned across the channel between two reed posts, the leaf still green and veined, sagging in the middle under a bead of water it gathered in the night, bowing any tall-masted boat.

A corner post: a pine cone stood upright on a flat river stone, lashed there with grass cord in four directions, a tuft of dried moss stuffed under each lashing where the cord was too loose, the stone already tilted one degree.

A petal curtain strung gate-wise between two rush stakes, overlapping triangles of scarlet poppy petal threaded on a root strand, each petal swinging in the stream-breath, one petal torn half through and flapping against its neighbour.

A mid-race drum station: an acorn-cap lashed brim-up to a hazel stake with bark-strip bands, a moss-padded seed beater leaning against it, a slender fae in woven grass breeches kneeling with one palm raised ready to strike.

A passage gate made from two crossed fern-frond ribs pegged into opposite banks, meeting overhead in an X, a threaded chain of linked clover strung along the crossing, the whole frame rippling whenever the current tugs its base pegs.
